title: The 352's Most Haunted: 7 places with spooky stories
site_name: 352today - Local News, Weather & Events in Ocala, FL
excerpt: From historic buildings and former hotels to a theater and an eerie stretch of road, these seven real places around the 352 have developed reputations for paranormal activity and spooky stories.
content:
From historic buildings and former hotels to a theater and an eerie stretch of road, these seven real places around the 352 have developed reputations for paranormal activity and spooky stories.

OCALA, FL (352today.com) – Every old town has its stories. In the 352, some of them just happen to come with a ghost.

From historic buildings and former hotels to a theater and a stretch of road with an eerie reputation, North Central Florida is home to places surrounded by tales of unexplained activity and lingering spirits.

Some stories have been passed down for generations. Others come from paranormal investigations or firsthand accounts. While there is no way to prove every ghost story, each one offers a glimpse into the history, folklore and sometimes downright strange stories attached to places across the region.

Hippodrome State Theatre

Before it became one of Gainesville’s best-known performing arts venues, the Hippodrome State Theater served as a federal courthouse and post office. The historic building at 25 SE 2nd Pl. has since become the setting for one of Gainesville’s more enduring ghost stories.

According to local legend, a man was once tried at the courthouse for a murder he did not commit. His wife reportedly had evidence that could have cleared him, but by the time she arrived in town, her husband had already been hanged. The story says the woman was devastated by his death and eventually lost her sanity. Today, legend holds that her spirit still searches the building for the man she was unable to save. One version of the story describes her as an apparition dressed in white.

The paranormal account is folklore rather than established history, with other sources identifying the tale as a submitted ghost story and notes that its paranormal accounts are largely unverifiable. The Hippodrome’s history as a former courthouse, however, is well documented.

While the story is fact, folklore or a little of both, the building’s past gives the legend an appropriately eerie setting.

Muse Cafe

An 1888 mansion in Ocala has developed its own ghost story. The building at 416 E. Fort King St., formerly associated with Muse Cafe, is reportedly home to the apparition of a woman dressed in old-fashioned clothing. According to a local report, the woman has been seen appearing on the mansion’s grand staircase. The account does not identify the woman or provide a documented historical event explaining her supposed presence.

That puts the story firmly in the realm of local paranormal folklore, but the building itself is real—and more than a century old. For a community with a substantial collection of historic homes and buildings, it’s perhaps fitting that some have acquired ghost stories along the way.

Panorama Inn/Silver Lake Lodge

The Panorama Inn and Silver Lake Lodge are no longer standing, but their story has managed to linger. The lakeside resort once stood at 501 Spring Lake Rd. in Silver Springs Shores. The property, originally known as Panorama Inn and later Silver Lake Lodge, was built as a resort overlooking Silver Lake and featured guest rooms, a swimming pool, dining facilities and a lakeside lounge.

By the end of the 1980s, the property had been abandoned. As the building deteriorated, it became a destination for urban explorers and thrill-seekers. Ghost stories eventually became part of the property’s reputation. Reports included flickering lights in empty rooms, strange noises and cold spots around the abandoned building. Paranormal accounts also describe local ghost hunters reporting doors that appeared to open and close on their own.

No known tragedies are tied to the property, meaning its reputation appears to have developed largely from the atmosphere of the abandoned building and reports from people who explored it. The Silver Lake Lodge was eventually demolished around 2006, leaving an empty lot where the resort once stood. The hotel may be gone, but photographs, memories and ghost stories have kept the former resort alive in local lore.

Ritz Historical Inn

The Ritz Historical Inn has been part of Ocala’s paranormal lore for years, but its ghost story comes with an important historical caveat. The building at 1205 E. Silver Springs Blvd. was constructed in 1925.

According to a Marion County Public Library publication, the Ritz became a popular gathering place during the Prohibition era. The publication also recounts local stories of a deadly fire at the property and claims that some believe the victims still haunt the former hotel. Other paranormal sources repeat the fire story, saying several guests died and their spirits remained behind.

That detail should be treated as legend rather than established history. Multiple reports note that the alleged fire is part of the building’s local lore and questions whether historical evidence exists to confirm it. The ghost stories themselves include reports of strange sensations and unexplained activity inside the building. There have also been accounts from visitors who say they experienced unusual occurrences during their time there.

The Ritz’s documented history and its legends have therefore become intertwined. There is a real historic building with a long past, but some of the darker details surrounding it remain difficult to separate from the folklore.

Seven Sisters Inn

The Seven Sisters Inn may be one of the 352’s best-known haunted locations. Located in Ocala’s historic district, the property is associated with the Rheinauer family. According to the inn’s own historical account, Charles Rheinauer was a prominent Ocala businessman who, along with his brother Maurice, established a retail dry goods business in the city. Charles and his wife, Emma, moved into the Victorian home in 1895. Charles later became the second Jewish person to serve as Ocala’s mayor.

The property’s reputation extends well beyond its architecture and history. A Marion County Public Library publication identifies Seven Sisters Inn as a local paranormal landmark and notes that it was featured on Syfy’s “Ghost Hunters.” According to the library, paranormal enthusiasts have reported several spirits at the property, including a spirit named George, described as a gentleman from the 1950s.

The inn’s appearance on “Ghost Hunters” also attracted attention beyond Ocala. Contemporary paranormal coverage reported that the television program planned to investigate claims of unexpected activity at the inn. Other accounts describe apparitions, unexplained voices and other unusual activity.

With its Victorian architecture, long history and television-famous reputation, Seven Sisters Inn has become something of a local celebrity among 352 ghost stories.

Thomas Hall

Some of Gainesville’s oldest ghost stories can be found right on the University of Florida campus. Thomas Hall was one of the first two buildings constructed at UF. According to the university’s history of its facilities, the building dates to 1905-06 and originally housed classrooms, laboratories, an auditorium, library, dining room and kitchen.

Its history eventually became intertwined with campus folklore. UF’s historical facilities publication documents the story of “Old Steve,” a campus cook whose kitchen was located beneath the classrooms and library in the center section of Thomas Hall. According to the legend, students could hear Steve shouting and cursing at his kitchen crew, along with the banging of pots and pans, hissing steam and crackling fire as he prepared lunch. The story says those sounds returned each fall when the campus steam heating system was turned on.

The legend has persisted for decades. A 2005 report in the Independent Florida Alligator noted that students continued to associate unexplained noises in Thomas Hall’s heating system with Old Steve. The same report also included a more mundane explanation from a UF official: The building simply had an old heating system. That makes Thomas Hall an interesting case where the ghost story itself is part of the documented history of the university—even if the ghost remains firmly in the realm of folklore.

Tiger Trail

Not every haunted location needs a building. In Dunnellon, “Tiger Trail” is the local name for SW 180th Avenue, a stretch of road that has developed an eerie reputation of its own. The road became particularly recognizable after portions of the 2001 horror movie “Jeepers Creepers” were filmed in the area. But the movie isn’t the only reason Tiger Trail has become associated with scary stories.

According to local lore, the ghosts of three children who were allegedly killed in a traffic accident appear along the road around 3 a.m. Some versions of the story say the children can be seen holding hands before before disappearing as approaching vehicles get closer. Other reported encounters describe shadowy figures and groups of people appearing along the roadside.

Sources identify the accounts as user-submitted ghost stories and notes that they are not scientifically verified. In fact, comments on the listing include people who claim to have seen the figures as well as others who say they have traveled the road repeatedly without experiencing anything unusual.

That disagreement is part of what makes Tiger Trail an interesting piece of local folklore. Whether the sightings are paranormal, misidentified shadows or simply a story that grew over time, the legend has become attached to the road.

The Stories that Stay Behind

The 352’s haunted places aren’t necessarily the ones with the most dramatic ghost stories. In many cases, their appeal comes from the history underneath the legend.

Some, like Thomas Hall and Seven Sisters Inn, are historic buildings with documented pasts and longstanding folklore. Others, like Panorama Inn, are places that have disappeared physically but remain in the memories and stories of people who knew them. And then there are locations such as Tiger Trail, where the legend itself has become part of the area’s identity.

Whether you’re a believer, a skeptic or somewhere in between, these stories offer another way to look at the places that make up the 352—because sometimes the history of a place is spooky enough all by itself.
